prompt:
Let $f\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be a continuously differentiable function. Prove that
$$\left|f(1)-\int_0^1f(x)\,dx\right|\le\frac12\max_{x\in[0,1]}|f'(x)| .$$

solutions.title: Integration by parts
solutions.body:
Since $f$ is $C^1$, integration by parts gives
$$\int_0^1x\,f'(x)\,dx=\big[x f(x)\big]_0^1-\int_0^1f(x)\,dx=f(1)-\int_0^1f(x)\,dx .$$
Let $K=\max_{[0,1]}|f'|$ (it exists, $f'$ being continuous on a compact interval). Then
$$\left|f(1)-\int_0^1f(x)\,dx\right|=\left|\int_0^1xf'(x)\,dx\right|\le\int_0^1x\,|f'(x)|\,dx\le K\int_0^1x\,dx=\frac K2 .$$
∎ (Equality holds for $f(x)=x$.)

solutions.title: Fundamental theorem of calculus and Fubini (official approach)
solutions.body:
Write $f(x)=f(0)+\int_0^xf'(y)\,dy$ and $f(1)=f(0)+\int_0^1f'(y)\,dy$. Then
$$f(1)-\int_0^1f(x)\,dx=\int_0^1f'(y)\,dy-\int_0^1\!\!\int_0^xf'(y)\,dy\,dx .$$
Swapping the order of integration in the double integral (the region is $0\le y\le x\le1$),
$$\int_0^1\!\!\int_0^xf'(y)\,dy\,dx=\int_0^1f'(y)\int_y^1dx\,dy=\int_0^1f'(y)(1-y)\,dy .$$
Hence $f(1)-\int_0^1f=\int_0^1f'(y)\big(1-(1-y)\big)dy=\int_0^1y\,f'(y)\,dy$, and the estimate finishes as in the first solution: $\left|\int_0^1yf'(y)\,dy\right|\le\max|f'|\cdot\frac12$. ∎

prompt:
Let $n$ be a positive integer and let $A,B$ be two complex nonsingular $n\times n$ matrices such that
$$A^2B-2ABA+BA^2=0 .$$
Prove that the matrix $AB^{-1}A^{-1}B-I_n$ is nilpotent. (Here $I_n$ denotes the $n\times n$ identity matrix. A matrix $X$ is called nilpotent if there exists a positive integer $k$ such that $X^k=0$.)
answer: The condition says $A$ commutes with $AB-BA$; from this, if $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of $X=AB^{-1}A^{-1}B$ then so is $2-\frac1\lambda$. This Möbius map is $u\mapsto u+1$ in the coordinate $u=\frac1{\lambda-1}$, so a finite spectrum forces $\lambda=1$; hence $X-I$ is nilpotent.

solutions.title: Eigenvalues are permuted by $\lambda\mapsto 2-1/\lambda$
solutions.body:
Let $X=AB^{-1}A^{-1}B$ and $C=AB-BA$. The hypothesis reads $A(AB-BA)-(AB-BA)A=0$, i.e. $AC=CA$; hence also $A^{-1}C=CA^{-1}$.

It suffices to show that $1$ is the only eigenvalue of $X$: then the characteristic polynomial of $X-I$ is $t^n$, and $(X-I)^n=0$ by Cayley–Hamilton.

**Lemma.** If $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of $X$, then $\mu=\frac{2\lambda-1}{\lambda}$ is also an eigenvalue of $X$.

*Proof.* $X$ is invertible, so $\lambda\ne0$, and $X-\lambda I$ is singular. Hence so is
$$BA^{-1}(X-\lambda I)=A^{-1}B-\lambda BA^{-1}.$$
We rewrite this using $C$: $\lambda A^{-1}(BA-AB)A^{-1}=\lambda A^{-1}B-\lambda BA^{-1}$, so
$$A^{-1}B-\lambda BA^{-1}=-\lambda A^{-1}CA^{-1}+(1-\lambda)A^{-1}B=-\lambda A^{-2}C+(1-\lambda)A^{-1}B,$$
using $CA^{-1}=A^{-1}C$. Multiplying on the left by the invertible matrix $\frac1\lambda B^{-1}A$:
$$\frac1\lambda B^{-1}A\big(-\lambda A^{-2}C+(1-\lambda)A^{-1}B\big)=-B^{-1}A^{-1}C+\frac{1-\lambda}{\lambda}I=B^{-1}A^{-1}BA-I+\frac{1-\lambda}\lambda I=Y-\mu I,$$
where $Y=B^{-1}A^{-1}BA$ and we used $-B^{-1}A^{-1}(AB-BA)=-I+B^{-1}A^{-1}BA$. So $Y-\mu I$ is singular, i.e. $\mu$ is an eigenvalue of $Y$. Finally $Y=A^{-1}XA$ is similar to $X$, so $\mu$ is an eigenvalue of $X$. $\square$

**Conclusion.** Let $\varphi(\lambda)=2-\frac1\lambda$. Note $\varphi(\lambda)-1=\frac{\lambda-1}{\lambda}$, so for $\lambda\ne1$ also $\varphi(\lambda)\ne1$ and
$$\frac1{\varphi(\lambda)-1}=\frac{\lambda}{\lambda-1}=\frac1{\lambda-1}+1 .$$
Suppose $X$ had an eigenvalue $\lambda_0\ne1$. By the lemma, $\lambda_k=\varphi^k(\lambda_0)$ are eigenvalues for all $k\ge0$, all $\ne1$, and $\frac1{\lambda_k-1}=\frac1{\lambda_0-1}+k$ are pairwise distinct. So $X$ would have infinitely many eigenvalues — impossible. Hence every eigenvalue of $X$ equals $1$, and $X-I_n=AB^{-1}A^{-1}B-I_n$ is nilpotent. ∎

prompt:
Let $n$ be a positive integer and let $G$ be a simple undirected graph on $n$ vertices. Let $d_i$ be the degree of its $i$-th vertex, $i=1,\dots,n$. Denote $\Delta=\max d_i$. Prove that if
$$\sum_{i=1}^nd_i^2>n\Delta(n-\Delta)$$
then $G$ contains a triangle. (A graph is called simple if there are no loops and no multiple edges between any pair of vertices.)
answer: If $G$ is triangle-free, adjacent vertices have disjoint neighbourhoods, so $d_i+d_j\le n$ on every edge and $\sum d_i^2=\sum_{ij\in E}(d_i+d_j)\le n|E|$; and $|E|\le\Delta(n-\Delta)$ because the neighbourhood of a max-degree vertex is independent.

solutions.title: Contrapositive: two counting bounds
solutions.body:
Assume $G$ has no triangle; we show $\sum d_i^2\le n\Delta(n-\Delta)$. Let $E$ be the edge set and $e=|E|$.

**Step 1: $\sum_id_i^2=\sum_{ij\in E}(d_i+d_j)$.** Each vertex $i$ appears in exactly $d_i$ edges and contributes $d_i$ to the right side for each of them, i.e. $d_i\cdot d_i$ in total.

**Step 2: $d_i+d_j\le n$ for every edge $ij$.** The neighbourhoods $N(i)$ and $N(j)$ are disjoint: a common neighbour $k$ would give a triangle $ijk$. Hence $d_i+d_j=|N(i)|+|N(j)|\le n$. With Step 1: $\sum_id_i^2\le n\,e$.

**Step 3: $e\le\Delta(n-\Delta)$.** Let $v$ have degree $\Delta$. No two vertices of $N(v)$ are adjacent (that would form a triangle with $v$), so every edge has at least one endpoint in $W=V\setminus N(v)$, a set of $n-\Delta$ vertices. Counting each edge from an endpoint in $W$,
$$e\le\sum_{w\in W}d_w\le(n-\Delta)\Delta .$$

Combining, $\sum_id_i^2\le ne\le n\Delta(n-\Delta)$. So if $\sum d_i^2>n\Delta(n-\Delta)$, $G$ must contain a triangle. ∎

(The bound is sharp: for the complete bipartite graph $K_{\Delta,\Delta}$ with $n=2\Delta$, $\sum d_i^2=2\Delta\cdot\Delta^2=n\Delta(n-\Delta)$.)

prompt:
Let $p>2$ be a prime and let
$$\mathcal A=\{n\in\mathbb N:\ 2p\mid n\ \text{and}\ p^2\nmid n\ \text{and}\ n\mid 3^n-1\}.$$
Prove that
$$\limsup_{k\to\infty}\frac{|\mathcal A\cap[1,k]|}{k}\le\frac{2\log3}{p\log p}.$$
answer: Write $n=pr$; Fermat gives $3^n\equiv3^r\pmod p$, so $l=\operatorname{ord}_p3$ divides $r$. Thus every $n\in\mathcal A$ is a multiple of $pl$, and $3^l>p$ gives $l>\frac{\log p}{\log3}$, so the density is at most $\frac1{pl}<\frac{\log3}{p\log p}$.

solutions.title: Order of 3 modulo $p$
solutions.body:
If $p=3$, no $n$ with $3\mid n$ divides $3^n-1$ (which is $\equiv2\pmod3$), so $\mathcal A=\emptyset$ and there is nothing to prove. Let $p\ge5$ and let $l$ be the multiplicative order of $3$ modulo $p$.

**Every $n\in\mathcal A$ is a multiple of $pl$.** Let $n\in\mathcal A$ and write $n=pr$ (possible as $p\mid n$). Since $p\mid n\mid3^n-1$, we have $3^n\equiv1\pmod p$. By Fermat's little theorem $3^p\equiv3\pmod p$, so
$$3^n=(3^p)^r\equiv3^r\pmod p,$$
hence $3^r\equiv1\pmod p$ and $l\mid r$. Therefore $pl\mid n$.

**Size of $l$.** $p\mid3^l-1$ and $3^l-1>0$, so $p\le3^l-1<3^l$, i.e. $l>\frac{\log p}{\log 3}$.

**Density.** $\mathcal A\cap[1,k]$ is contained in the set of multiples of $pl$ in $[1,k]$, which has at most $\frac k{pl}$ elements. Hence
$$\limsup_{k\to\infty}\frac{|\mathcal A\cap[1,k]|}{k}\le\frac1{pl}<\frac{\log3}{p\log p}\le\frac{2\log3}{p\log p}.$$
∎ (Neither the condition $p^2\nmid n$ nor the evenness of $n$ is needed for this bound; the official solution uses them to get $3^{r/2}\equiv\pm1\pmod p$, which leads to the factor $2$.)
